1.66000,28.03000.desc: A decision on a living modified organism, filed by the country itself to the Biosafety Clearing-House. Article 20 of the Cartagena Protocol requires every party to file its release and market decisions there within fifteen days, and 173 parties are bound by it. The United States is not among them. Nowhere else holds national release decisions from this many countries in one place. A country with no records here has not necessarily approved nothing — it may not have filed, and from the outside those two look the same.

-96.77440,32.91270.name: The Center for Reproductive Endocrinology
-96.77440,32.91270.desc: A fertility clinic reporting to the CDC's National ART Surveillance System. Medical director: Walid A. Saleh, MD. A fertility clinic is where human embryos are made, selected and stored, and where assisted reproduction happens, like IVF, ICSI, egg and sperm donation, freezing embryos and eggs for later. Reporting is required of every US clinic performing assisted reproduction, under the Fertility Clinic Success Rate and Certification Act, so this is close to a complete register rather than a list of members. What it records is cycles started, which is not the same as children born.

What that project could not find out is absent here too.

-6.84160,34.02090.name: Office National de Sécurité Sanitaire des Produits Alimentaires
-6.84160,34.02090.desc: Morocco’s food safety authority, in a country that imports engineered feed without permitting cultivation. North African import policy determines what North American and South American exporters plant, at a scale rarely credited to the importing countries.

-77.04510,38.90410.name: Alliance for Regenerative Medicine — sector data
-77.04510,38.90410.desc: The trade body for cell and gene therapy, and the source of the financing, trial and pipeline figures almost every account of the sector uses — including this map's. An industry association counting its own field is the only systematic count that exists, because no regulator publishes one, and the numbers therefore come with the interests of the people compiling them.

6.84200,46.46000.name: Nestlé
6.84200,46.46000.desc: The largest food company in the world, and a buyer whose sourcing specifications reach millions of hectares. When a manufacturer of this size says it will not accept engineered ingredients in a market, growers in that supply chain stop planting them — a decision taken commercially, with no consultation and no appeal.

-92.28960,34.74650.name: Arkansas State Plant Board
-92.28960,34.74650.desc: A state regulator that restricted a federally approved product, and was sued for it. After nearly a thousand complaints in 2017 — affecting some 800,000 acres of soybeans alone — it halted in-crop dicamba use by emergency order in July, then voted to bar it from 16 April to 31 October 2018. It held seventeen meetings on the herbicide that year. It also rejected the company's petition, and rejected a further petition seeking to disqualify a board member who represented the state seed growers' association and had solicited support for the cutoff date; he said openly that he saw it as part of representing seed growers. Later boards moved the cutoff to 25 May. The entry matters because sub-national regulators are almost absent from this map, and here one set the binding constraint on a product two federal agencies had approved.

-92.28960,34.74650.name: Monsanto Co. v. Arkansas State Plant Board
-92.28960,34.74650.state: Little Rock — Pulaski County Circuit Court and the Supreme Court of Arkansas
-92.28960,34.74650.desc: The company sued the state board in October 2017, arguing it had exceeded its delegated authority, had failed to consider the research submitted to federal regulators, and that the statute creating the board was an unconstitutional delegation of power. A group of Arkansas farmers sued separately over the same rules. The circuit court dismissed the company's case on sovereign immunity in February 2018; the state supreme court held in 2019 that the claims could be brought, by which time the contested rules had expired and been replaced, so those parts were dismissed as moot while the constitutional question and the research requirement went back down. Two things are visible here that appear nowhere else on this map: a company litigating against a regulator rather than the reverse, and a rule surviving simply by expiring before the challenge concluded.
